title: Modern DevOps Practices
description: Implement modern DevOps practices using GitHub Actions, OIDC, automated deployments, blue/green, canary, and feature flags.

data.text: Modern DevOps combines culture, automation, and tooling to deliver software faster and more reliably. On AWS, this means using GitHub Actions or AWS CodePipeline with OIDC authentication, automated testing, and progressive deployment strategies.

GitHub Actions is a popular CI/CD platform. You can connect it to AWS using OIDC (OpenID Connect) to authenticate without storing long-lived AWS access keys. OIDC uses short-lived tokens that are automatically rotated, making your pipeline more secure.

With OIDC, GitHub exchanges a short-lived token for temporary AWS credentials. You configure an IAM OIDC identity provider in AWS and a trust policy that allows GitHub actions to assume specific IAM roles. This eliminates the need to store AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY in GitHub secrets.
Deploying all at once (big bang) risks downtime. Progressive deployment strategies release changes gradually, reducing blast radius and giving you time to detect issues.

data.title: Progressive Deployment Strategies
items: **Blue/Green** — deploy the new version to a separate environment, then switch traffic. Fast rollback by switching back.
**Canary** — shift a small percentage of traffic (e.g., 5%) to the new version, monitor, then gradually increase.
**Linear** — shift traffic in fixed increments over time (10% every 10 minutes)
**Feature flags** — deploy code with new features hidden behind flags, enabling them for specific users

data.title: GitHub Actions Workflow with OIDC
data.content: A GitHub Actions workflow that deploys to AWS using OIDC instead of access keys.
data.code:
name: Deploy to AWS

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  id-token: write
  contents: read

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      
      - name: Configure AWS credentials
        uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/GitHubActionsRole
          aws-region: us-east-1
      
      - name: Build and test
        run: |
          npm ci
          npm test
      
      - name: Deploy to Lambda
        run: |
          aws lambda update-function-code \
            --function-name my-function \
            --zip-file fileb://dist/lambda.zip

data.title: OIDC is More Secure
data.text: OIDC replaces long-lived AWS access keys with short-lived, automatically rotated tokens. This is the recommended approach for GitHub Actions and other CI/CD tools.

terms.definition: OpenID Connect — a standard for exchanging short-lived tokens between GitHub and AWS, eliminating the need for long-lived access keys.
A deployment strategy that shifts a small percentage of traffic to the new version before full rollout.
A conditional switch that hides new features behind a toggle, allowing you to enable or disable them without deploying code.
A deployment strategy that runs two identical environments and switches traffic from old (blue) to new (green).

data.title: Set Up GitHub Actions with OIDC
data.description: Configure an IAM OIDC identity provider in AWS and create a GitHub Actions workflow that deploys a Lambda function.
steps: Create an OIDC identity provider in AWS IAM for GitHub
Create an IAM role with a trust policy allowing GitHub to assume it
Attach a policy that grants Lambda deployment permissions
Create a GitHub Actions workflow with the `aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials` action
Push a code change and watch the pipeline deploy
data.expectedOutcome: Your Lambda function is deployed by GitHub Actions using OIDC, with no long-lived AWS keys stored in GitHub secrets.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: OIDC lets GitHub Actions authenticate to AWS without long-lived keys
Blue/Green and canary deployments reduce release risk
Feature flags decouple deployment from feature release
Automated testing and security scanning belong in every pipeline
data.takeaway: Modern DevOps is about fast, safe, and automated deployments. OIDC, progressive rollouts, and feature flags are the tools that make it possible.
